title: Insert a given node in BST
statement:
Given the **root** node of a binary search tree (BST) and a value **val** to insert into the tree. Return the **root **nodeof the BST after the insertion.

It is guaranteed that the new value does not exist in the original BST. Note that the compiler output shows true if the node is added correctly, else false.

**Example 1:**

```
Input : root = [4, 2, 7, 1, 3] , val = 5
Output : [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 5]
Explanation :
Below is image where the node 5 is inserted
![](https://static.takeuforward.org/content/1789455495_jIB-bKGk.webp)
There is another way to insert the given val as shown below.
![](https://static.takeuforward.org/content/1789455503_rYfApE4i.webp)
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input : root = [40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70] , val = 25
Output : [40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70, null, null, 25]
Explanation :
Below is image where the node 25 is inserted
![](https://static.takeuforward.org/content/1789455510_kSZGKb_9.webp)
```
constraints:
- 1 <= Number of nodes <= 10^4
- -10^8 <= Node.val <= 10^8
- All values in tree are **unique**.
- -10^8 <= val <= 10^8
- It is guaranteed that the val does not exists in original BST.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.body: If root == null, create a new node with val and return it. If val < root.val, insert val into the left subtree (root.left). If val > root.val, insert val into the right subtree (root.right). Return the root node after insertion.

hints.title: Hint 2
hints.body: Start from the root and traverse the tree. If val < current.val, move left. If val > current.val, move right. When an empty spot (null) is found, create a new node and attach it. Return the original root.

doubts.question: What happens if the BST is skewed?
doubts.answer: If the BST is left-heavy, inserting a large value will extend it further right. If it is right-heavy, inserting a small value will extend it further left.

doubts.question: Can we balance the tree after insertion?
doubts.answer: Standard BST insertion does not balance the tree. To ensure balanced insertion, use AVL trees or Red-Black Trees, which rebalance after insertions.

followUps.question: How does this problem relate to databases and indexing?
followUps.answer: BSTs are the basis for B-Trees, used in database indexing. Balanced insertions ensure efficient search, insert, and delete operations in structured storage systems.

followUps.question: How would you modify this for self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black Trees)?
followUps.answer: After insertion, perform rotations and balance updates to maintain a logarithmic height. AVL trees ensure balance immediately, while Red-Black trees allow temporary imbalance.

facts: Binary search tree insertion models how ordered sets and maps maintain searchable in-memory indexes, such as symbol tables and scheduling queues.
Many standard-library ordered containers use balanced BST variants, preserving BST ordering while preventing insertion patterns from making searches inefficient.

peerSolutions.title: Python parent-link insertion for a BST
peerSolutions.author: Yash Chauhan
peerSolutions.content:
This keeps both the current node and its parent. Once the search reaches `None`, the parent tells us whether the new value belongs on the left or right. It also makes the root insertion case easy to handle before the loop.

```python
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode(object):
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.data = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right

class Solution:
    def insertIntoBST(self, root, val):
        new_node = TreeNode(val)

        if root is None:
            return new_node

        parent = None
        current = root

        while current is not None:
            parent = current
            if val < current.data:
                current = current.left
            else:
                current = current.right

        if val < parent.data:
            parent.left = new_node
        else:
            parent.right = new_node

        return root
```

The edge cases are an empty tree and inserting a value into a leaf. In both cases, the new node is linked without rebuilding any part of the tree.

The original tree is modified by setting one child reference. For a skewed tree, the loop may visit every node, while a balanced tree needs only a few levels.

Time complexity: `O(h)`.
Space complexity: `O(1)`.
